title: Welcome to Mooseport
full_review:
All's fair in love and politics is the theme of the lukewarm comedy "Welcome to Mooseport" (20th Century Fox). The film is part triangular romance, part political satire, and the odds of director Donald Petrie's farce winning a landslide at the box office are about as slim as Dennis Kucinich delivering a State of the Union address.

TV funnyman Ray Romano stars as Handy Harrison, an aloof fix-it man who owns a mom-and-pop hardware store in the quaint New England town of Mooseport, Maine.

Gene Hackman plays Monroe "Eagle" Cole, the wildly popular outgoing U.S. president who decides to pitch his tent in the idyllic hamlet once he leaves office. Cole arrives in town, eager to retire to a life of leisure and lucrative speaking engagements while he licks his wounds over his recent messy divorce. But no sooner has the Eagle landed than Cole is approached by the town council, asking him to run for mayor.

But his campaign trail takes an unexpected turn when Harrison tosses his hat into the ring and announces his candidacy after Cole makes a pass at the handyman's veterinarian-girlfriend (Maura Tierney), turning the quiet town of Mooseport on its antlers.

While it makes some witty observations about the electoral process and the media's scrutiny of candidates' private lives, the film fails to make good on its campaign promise of comedy. In fact what starts out as a promising premise ends up as politics as usual -- early expectations quickly deflated. And though much of the humor is laced with cynicism, "Mooseport" is fueled by a Capraesque belief in the basic goodness and decency of Main Street America.

The easygoing Romano is likable but his what-you-see-is-what-you-get talent seems better suited for the small screen. As always, Hackman is a pleasure to watch, bringing a well-honed professionalism that elevates even the most mediocre material and raises the performance levels of everyone else in the scene. The same goes for the chameleonic Marcia Gay Harden, who plays Cole's lovelorn chief of staff.

Christine Baranski injects some much-needed energy into the mix as Cole's ex-wife, whom he refers to as the "Wicked Witch of the West Wing" and who bears a coiffed resemblance to another ambitious former first lady. Occasional laughs are also provided by Rip Torn as Cole's wacky campaign manager, as well as by the commander-in-chief's overzealous Secret Service handlers.

In one scene the ex-prez's baby-faced PR director (Fred Savage) advises Cole that a sense of humor would help him in the polls, informing him, "Funny is your weakness." It is also the film's weakness. And while none of this is an impeachable offense, one may want to veto seeing "Mooseport" until it comes out on video. Besides, there is another campaign coming up that will probably provide loads more laughs.

Due to some sexual humor, instances of rear nudity, and minimal crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
